resumeBlocs: OPESc+ is an observatory of world economic indicators. It collects, harmonises and makes available the series published by the major international statistical institutions, so that analysis carried out within the ministry rests on a common, traceable and up-to-date base.
The tool rests on five principles.
No locally produced data. The platform computes and estimates nothing. It passes on what the World Bank, the International Monetary Fund and Harvard University's Growth Lab publish, unaltered.
Never offer a filter that leads nowhere. The frequencies offered, the countries listed and the period bounds are those that actually exist in the database for the chosen indicator.
A missing value is information. It is never stored as zero, never interpolated, and a series with gaps is drawn as a dashed line.
Traceable collection. Every run is logged, and every export carries its sources and retrieval date.
Data and interpretation kept apart. The projections offered are mechanical extensions, explicitly presented as such.
What OPESc+ is, and what it is not

OPESc+ is a tool for consulting, comparing and reporting. It is not a macroeconomic model: it simulates no shock, computes no scenario and produces no institutional forecast. The three projection methods it offers are statistical extensions of the observed series, with no policy assumption. For shock simulation and reference projections, the tool is OPESc, which OPESc+ complements.

blocs: consult economic series for every economy in the world;
compare several countries or several indicators on one chart;
read a geographic distribution on a world map;
extend a series using three documented statistical methods;
export charts, maps and data for use in a note;
maintain a base updated automatically from the providers.

The chain has four stages. Connectors query the providers' public interfaces. The collection engine harmonises country codes, periods and units, then writes to a single database. The interface reads that database and never writes to it. Exports produce standalone files carrying their sources.
This separation has a practical consequence: consulting the platform can never alter the data, and a collection in progress does not prevent consultation.
Further indicators appear in the catalogue without being active: their provider has no connector yet. They are deactivated at load time rather than left visible and silent in the interface.
World Development Indicators, International Debt Statistics, governance, poverty, Findex, logistics performance

The data remain the property of their producers. Harvard University's Growth Lab, the OECD and the International Monetary Fund explicitly require attribution. Every exported workbook carries a Sources sheet stating, for each indicator, its origin and the retrieval date. Never circulate an extract without that sheet.

Why the manual language is asked for

It is not inferred from the interface language. A staff member using the platform in French may need the English version for a technical or financial partner, and the other way round. The form offers the current language by default, without imposing it.

Why the cascades follow the first indicator

When several indicators are selected, the frequency, period and country list follow the first one. Combining them across all indicators would produce intersections that are often empty, and an empty filter is more confusing than a truncated secondary series. Check that your main indicator comes first in the selection.

Two routes lead to the same result. Select several indicators at once in the list, then apply. Or build a selection, add it to the chart, compose another and add it in turn: that is the route for crossing indicators from different categories.
Each displayed series appears as a chip, removed with one click on the cross. The ceiling is six series.

When the displayed series do not share a unit, they are automatically rebased to 100 at their first observation. Overlaying a share of gross domestic product and a price in dollars per tonne on one axis would flatten one of the two beyond readability. The Base 100 box forces that treatment even when units agree, to compare relative movements rather than levels.

It keeps only the last displayed period, whose year appears in the title, and discards zero or negative values. Above all, it sums what it shows. For exports in dollars, that total means something. For shares of gross domestic product, indices or ranks, it means nothing: the platform still draws the chart but displays a warning. Do not circulate it in that case.
A series with gaps is drawn as a dashed line and never interpolated: joining two points several years apart with a solid line would suggest a movement that was not observed.
Three extension methods are offered, each with its interval. They apply to the first selected country and require at least five annual observations.

They are mechanical extensions of the observed series. They embed no policy assumption, no shock and no information outside the series itself. They must never be presented as a ministry forecast. For a macroeconomic framework, the tool is OPESc.

The Image button produces a PNG file on a white background at print resolution, ready to paste into a note. The Data button produces a workbook holding exactly the displayed selection, with its sources sheet.

Below the chart, a world map shades countries by the indicator's value for a year chosen with the slider. A play button steps through the years automatically, showing a dynamic the chart cannot when countries are numerous.
The map follows the first displayed indicator. Overlaying several indicators on one colour scale would make no sense, as the units are not comparable.

The scale is capped at the 2nd and 98th percentiles of the distribution. Without that precaution, a few extreme values would give every other country the same shade: on public debt, a handful of countries above 200 per cent of gross domestic product would flatten the whole reading. The tooltip always shows the real, uncapped value.
Regional aggregates are excluded from the map as from rankings. Countries in your selection are outlined more heavily.

Clicking a country opens its panel on the right: flag, official language, region, income group, indicator value and world rank for the displayed year. The Ranking button exports the full ranking for that year.
Where the country details come from

The two-letter codes and official languages of 216 countries come from no statistical source: they are maintained by hand in a project file, editable without touching the code. A country missing from that table shows empty fields rather than breaking the map.

This tab answers a daily difficulty: finding a figure or a publication without getting lost among results whose origin and worth are unclear.

The principle is the opposite of a general search engine. The list of sources is closed and chosen, and the search covers only those. Thirty-five sources across three natures: seventeen data providers, nine publishers, nine news outlets. Four are Cameroonian: the National Institute of Statistics, MINEPAT, the Ministry of Finance and the Autonomous Sinking Fund.
The definition of the notion, when it appears in the platform glossary. Forty-four economic notions are defined, from gross domestic product to the structural balance.

The sources to query directly, at most six, chosen for their relevance to the topic.
Why six sources and not thirty-five

Showing every source on every query would amount to no filtering at all. Only those that genuinely cover the topic are kept. Ranking crosses three criteria: the category's rank in the query, that category's rank at the site, and the site's specialisation. At equal rank, a site covering three domains is more relevant than a portal covering eight.

From two characters onwards, a completion list appears below the field. It draws on the glossary, the fourteen categories and the indicator labels: suggestions therefore cover what the platform can actually handle, not a general dictionary.

Every indicator shown carries its definition and, below it, the name of the institution that stands behind it. The World Bank publishes, for each of its series, a definition text and the organisation that establishes it: both are reproduced as they stand.

For general notions, the glossary definitions point to the manual they are drawn from: the System of National Accounts for gross domestic product, the Balance of Payments Manual for the current account, the resolutions of the International Conference of Labour Statisticians for unemployment.
Why the source is always named

A definition without a source is worth nothing in an administrative document: the World Bank's commits the World Bank, an anonymous one commits no one. It also lets the reference be cited in a note without having to look it up.

Without configuration, the tab offers the sources to query, each link running the search on the target site. To get results directly, a programmable search engine is needed, free of charge, restricted to the platform's domains.

The command `domaines_pour_moteur()` prints the thirty domains to declare, and `configurer_recherche()` stores the identifiers. The full procedure is in chapter 9 of the project README.

Even when the engine is restricted to included sites, the platform filters results against the domain list before displaying them. A configuration mistake must not be enough to let an arbitrary source in. Subdomains are accepted, imitations rejected.
The platform updates itself by querying its providers' public interfaces. Every run is logged with its scope, trigger, status, the number of values added and revised, and the details of any errors.

A collection can end without error and bring back nothing, for instance if a provider has renamed a code. Without a log, that silent failure would go unnoticed for months and analysis would rest on frozen series. Check the log after every update.
From the Data collection tab, for one category or for the whole catalogue. A full collection means several hundred calls and takes thirty to forty-five minutes: proceed one category at a time.

Two to four revisions a year

Not every source can be queried programmatically. The International Monetary Fund's Primary Commodity Price System page builds its download link in JavaScript: no address appears in the page source, so it cannot be found automatically.
The platform takes two measures for this case, which is not rare.
The file shipped with the platform

Commodity prices are distributed inside the package and loaded at initialisation, just like the catalogue. No command to run: after `preparer_base()`, the 108 products of category C15 are in place, at monthly, quarterly and annual frequency.
Loading overwrites nothing if it finds existing data: a more recent file you imported yourself stays in place.

The Data collection tab includes a drop area. Choose a file and a category, and the series it holds join that category. Those unknown to the catalogue are created automatically, with the source's own label.

Reading is tolerant: columns are identified by their content as much as by their heading. The wide format, one row per series and one column per period, is recognised, the frequency being read from the column name.
An imported figure is worth a collected one

It uses the same writing function, carries the same frequencies and feeds the same counters. An indicator is active if it can be fed or already is: an imported series therefore stays visible and usable, even though it has no connector. Data present is data usable, however it arrived.

Category C15 gathers the 108 products of the downloaded file: aggregate indices, precious metals and energy transition metals, rare earths, cereals, oilseeds, meats, seafood, timber, fertilisers, teas by origin.

A narrower category, limited to twenty-eight main quotations, existed at first. It has been removed: it duplicated the other, and its automatic feed never succeeded. A complete category is worth more than a partial duplicate.

Fourteen series from the file are set aside on import. They are exchange rates, recognisable by their code, and have no place in a category of products. They remain available in the exchange rate category.

Every observation is placed on the first day of the period it covers: 1 January for a year, the first day of the quarter, the first day of the month. This convention is what allows series of different frequencies to be overlaid on one chart.
Commodity prices are collected monthly and also aggregated into annual averages; otherwise they would share no frequency with annual indicators and could not be compared.

The aggregation used is the arithmetic mean of the months in the year. A price is a period average: summing twelve monthly quotations would produce no interpretable quantity. For a flow, such as monthly exports, the sum would be the rule; the current catalogue holds none.

Each series is divided by its first non-missing observation within the displayed period, then multiplied by one hundred. A series whose first value is zero or missing is dropped from the chart rather than producing infinite values that would flatten the other curves.
All three methods rely solely on the annual observations available for the chosen country.
The linear trend fits a straight line by ordinary least squares and extends it. The interval is built from the standard deviation of the residuals.

The random walk with drift takes the mean change over the last five periods and adds it to the last observed value, once per horizon step. Uncertainty grows with the square root of the horizon, reflecting the accumulation of successive errors.

Holt smoothing updates a level and a trend at each period, each weighted between the new observation and the previous extrapolation. It therefore reacts faster to recent turning points than the linear trend.
The colour bounds are the 2nd and 98th percentiles of the value distribution for the displayed year, aggregates excluded. Values beyond take the extreme shade without stretching the scale.

A missing value is never stored. The absence of a row means absence of data, never zero. Providers nonetheless return a row for every country-period pair, including where there is no data: on an indicator with sparse coverage, more than nine tenths of the volume would be empty rows.
As a result, a series with gaps is drawn as a dashed line with visible points, and never interpolated.

Providers do not use the same coding. The country table keeps, for each economy, the reference identifier and those specific to each source. Without that mapping, joins would produce incomplete series with no error raised.

Macroeconomic data are revised. A 2023 gross domestic product figure collected in January may differ from the same figure collected in June. The platform keeps the latest known value and the collection date, with no vintage history. A published note must therefore carry its retrieval date.

The Economic Complexity Index is not measured but computed across all countries and products simultaneously. A revision to one large exporter's trade data mechanically shifts every other country's index. Values are therefore not comparable from one Atlas release to the next.
Furthermore, a year's trade data reach the Atlas only about two years later: the latest available year will always lag the rest of the dashboard by that much.

They are read directly from the provider's workbook rather than copied. They may therefore differ from other publications: cocoa is quoted per kilogram in the Pink Sheet and per tonne in some sources. Always check the unit shown on the axis before quoting a level.

The schema provides for weekly, daily and intraday steps, but no catalogue source feeds them. This is not a limitation of the tool: a quarterly gross domestic product has no daily value. Those steps only make sense for market data, which come from other providers and are often paid.

The World Bank, which supplies most of the active indicators, publishes annual data only. The only monthly series in the catalogue are commodity prices. If the frequency filter offers nothing but Annual, that is not a fault: no sub-annual series has been collected.
